narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 91.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and wants students likely to pass, this strong prediction of failure led to your application being rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class ranking at the end of your third year in law school was the single biggest reason the model expected you to fail. Standing in the bottom decile (compared to an average of about 5.8 among accepted students) strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year class ranking was the second most important factor and also worked against you. Being in the lowest decile (versus an average around 6 for accepted students) added further weight toward expecting you to struggle on the bar.

Your family’s upper-middle income level was the third most influential piece of information. While this is the most common income bracket among accepted students, in your specific case it still nudged the model slightly toward predicting failure rather than success.

Taken together, these academic performance signals were powerful enough that the model became very confident you would not pass the bar on the first try.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking key courses, seeking targeted tutoring for the bar, or gaining additional practical legal experience before reapplying. Improving your class standing and test preparation can meaningfully change future predictions. (218 words)
